title: Trojan ticket concept and LTH-based pruning regime for Trojan models
content: A Trojan ticket is defined as a sparse subnetwork $(m\odot\theta)$ obtained by applying iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) to a trained model $\theta$ that was learned on a potentially poisoned dataset $\mathcal{D}_\mathrm{p}$, where $m\in\{0,1\}^d$ is the binary pruning mask and $\odot$ denotes elementwise product. The proposed LTH-oriented regime for Trojan analysis uses IMP cycles (train dense model on $\mathcal{D}_\mathrm{p}$; prune $p\%$ by magnitude per round; update mask $m$) and examines both (a) the un-rewound pruned subnetwork $(m\odot\theta)$ and (b) its $k$-step finetuned variant $(m\odot\theta^{(k)})$ (where $\theta^{(k)}$ denotes $k$ gradient steps of finetuning under $\mathcal{D}_\mathrm{p}$, e.g., $k=10$). This regime intentionally avoids using any clean dataset for pruning or finetuning so that the sparsity-induced behavior reflects the interaction between pruning and Trojan-encoded parameters rather than effects of clean-data finetuning.

title: LMC-based Trojan score to quantify pruning-induced stability and detect Trojan presence
content: In the specific iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) regime adopted for Trojan analysis — where after each pruning round the surviving weights are not rewound to their initialization and all finetuning uses only the potentially poisoned dataset $\mathcal{D}_\mathrm{p}$ (no clean data) — the Trojan score is defined to quantify the pruning-induced stability of Trojan tickets by measuring the linear-mode connectivity (LMC) error barrier between the un-finetuned Trojan ticket $(m\odot\theta)$ and the $k$-step finetuned Trojan ticket $(m\odot\theta^{(k)})$. Here, $\theta$ are the parameters of the dense model trained on $\mathcal{D}_\mathrm{p}$, $m\in\{0,1\}^d$ is the binary pruning mask, $\odot$ denotes elementwise product, and $\theta^{(k)}$ denotes $\theta$ after $k$ gradient steps of finetuning on $\mathcal{D}_\mathrm{p}$. Given a model training error functional $\mathcal{E}(\cdot)$ evaluated on $\mathcal{D}_\mathrm{p}$, the LMC error barrier is $$e_{\sup}(\phi_1,\phi_2)=\max_{\alpha\in[0,1]}\mathcal{E}(\alpha\phi_1+(1-\alpha)\phi_2).$$ Setting $\phi_1 = m\odot\theta$ and $\phi_2 = m\odot\theta^{(k)}$, the Trojan score is $$\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}} \;=\; e_{\sup}(m\odot\theta,\;m\odot\theta^{(k)}) \;-\; \frac{\mathcal{E}(m\odot\theta)+\mathcal{E}(m\odot\theta^{(k)})}{2}.$$ Under the described IMP regime, the Trojan score is approximately zero for non-Trojan (clean) models because the linear interpolation error barrier equals the average of the endpoints' errors. A significantly positive peak in $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ along the pruning path indicates an atypical pruning stability fingerprint associated with a backdoor. Therefore, computing $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ along the IMP pruning path yields a data-free detector that identifies pruning levels where Trojan information is isolated.

title: Existence of a winning Trojan ticket that preserves attack success under extreme sparsity
content: Empirically, across multiple architectures (ResNet-20s, ResNet-18, VGG-16, DenseNet-100) and datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Restricted ImageNet) and for diverse Trojan types (gray-scale patch, RGB patch, clean-label, stealthier WaNet), there exists an extreme-sparsity subnetwork—termed the winning Trojan ticket—identified by a peak in the Trojan score (the LMC-based metric $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ that quantifies pruning-induced stability via the error barrier between un-finetuned and finetuned Trojan tickets), which simultaneously (i) preserves the Trojan attack effectiveness in terms of attack success rate (ASR) nearly as well as the original dense Trojan model and (ii) has near-random standard accuracy (SA) on clean inputs due to the aggressive pruning. For example, for ResNet-20s on CIFAR-10 with an RGB trigger, at very extreme sparsity the winning Trojan ticket exhibited ASR = 94.49% while SA dropped to 11.38%; across experiments, winning-ticket ASR values reached 99.6% for RGB triggers and 99.8% for clean-label triggers. The winning Trojan ticket is consistently associated with the peak Trojan score along IMP.

title: Data-free reverse engineering of triggers using the winning Trojan ticket yields substantially improved target-label detection and recovered-trigger attack success
content:
Using the winning Trojan ticket as the victim model in a trigger-recovery optimization
      $$
      \min_{z\in\{0,1\}^n,\;\delta}\; \mathbb{E}_x\big[\ell_{\mathrm{atk}}(x'(z,\delta);\phi,t)\big] + \gamma\,h(z,\delta),
      $$
      with $x'(z,\delta)=(1-z)\odot x + z\odot\delta$, C\&W targeted loss $\ell_{\mathrm{atk}}$, and the regularizer $h$ from prior work, and solving the label-wise optimizations followed by selecting the label with minimum $\|z^*\odot\delta^*\|_1$ recovers (i) the correct Trojan target label more reliably than applying the same optimization to the dense model and (ii) a recovered trigger that, when stamped onto test images, achieves substantially higher ASR. Representative quantitative results: on ResNet-20s, CIFAR-10, (a) gray-scale trigger: recovered ASR = 91.2% (winning ticket) vs 71.4% (dense baseline); (b) RGB trigger: 99.6% vs 48.0%; (c) clean-label trigger: 99.8% vs 9.6% (an over 90%-point ASR improvement reported). The recovered triggers from winning Trojan tickets are effective even when the recovery optimization uses only 100 Gaussian noise images as base inputs (i.e., "for free") rather than any clean images.
